title: The NPM Package Manager and Installing External Node Modules
summary: Explains what npm is, how to initialise a project with npm init to get package.json, how to install and use a third-party package (sillyname), and how to switch a project to ES modules with "type": "module". The exercise is to install the superheroes package and print a random hero name.

concepts.heading: What npm is
points: npm (Node Package Manager) is a public, open-source registry of reusable modules written by other developers, run by GitHub. It is shared code you pull in instead of writing everything yourself.
Native modules are the built-in toolbox; npm packages are the community library of extra tools you add when a task needs one.
npm is installed together with Node, so no separate install is needed.
Packages are searched on npmjs.com. Each package page shows the install command and usage examples.

concepts.heading: Initialising a project with npm init
points: cd into the project folder first, then run npm init. It starts an interactive wizard that produces package.json.

Prompts in order: package name (lecture uses learning-npm), version (default 1.0.0), description, entry point (default index.js), test command, git repository, keywords, author, license (default ISC). Pressing Enter keeps defaults/leaves blank.
At the end the wizard prints the JSON it will write and asks for confirmation; answer y.
package.json is a plain JSON file of key/value pairs describing the project. On its own it is only configuration; it becomes useful once packages are installed.
(Extra) npm init -y accepts every default without prompting.

concepts.heading: Installing and using a package
points: Install with npm install <package-name>. The shorthand npm i does the same. Several packages can be installed at once by listing names separated by spaces.
Installing adds a dependencies section to package.json recording the package name and version range, and creates a node_modules folder holding the downloaded package code (and its own dependencies).
(Extra) Also generated: package-lock.json, which pins exact resolved versions. node_modules is normally excluded from git and can be rebuilt with npm install.
Usage steps: read the package's npm page, import it, call the function it exposes. For sillyname the exported function generates a random funny name.
The lecture first uses the older CommonJS pattern, var generateName = require("sillyname"), then calls generateName() and logs the result in a template literal (backticks with ${} interpolation).
Run the file with node index.js to see a different silly name each time.

concepts.heading: CommonJS vs ES modules
points: CJS (CommonJS) is the original Node system based on require(). ESM (ECMAScript modules) uses import/from and is the standard shared with front-end JavaScript. Node has supported ESM since about version 12.
To enable ESM in a project, add a top-level key in package.json: "type": "module". The default value is commonjs. The lecture places it just under "main".
ESM syntax: import name from "package". Typing the module path first (import {  } from "pkg") lets VS Code autocomplete the exported names; typing the name first gives no suggestions.
Once import is used, the old require line can be deleted.

concepts.heading: (Extra) Reference repo notes
points: (Extra) The reference script.js uses the current named import (import { randomSuperhero } from 'superheroes') with superheroes ^4.0.0 in package.json, while its solution.js still uses the old default import and superheroes.random(), which throws with v4.
(Extra) Its solution.js imports "sillyName" with a capital N; the npm name is all lowercase, sillyname.

cd path/to/project
npm init
npm i sillyname
node index.js

task.name: Superhero name generator
task.starting_point: The same npm project and index.js used for sillyname, with package.json already set to "type": "module".
task.goal: Use the superheroes package to print a random hero name in the console.
steps: Find the superheroes package on npmjs.com (a link is in the course resources) and read its usage section.
In the project folder run npm i superheroes and confirm it appears under dependencies in package.json.
Comment out the sillyname code in index.js (or keep it; both can run in the same file).
Import the package at the top of index.js. With the current version this is a named import: import { randomSuperhero } from "superheroes"; (the package name string must match exactly).
Generate a name with const name = randomSuperhero(); (the video's older version used superheroes.random() on a default import).
console.log a sentence such as I am <name>! using a template literal: console.log(`I am ${name}!`).
Run node index.js; each run should print a different hero.
task.expected_result: Console output like: I am Piledriver! (different each run).
task.reference_repo_path: Section 23 - Node.js/23.03 - The NPM Package Manager and Installing External Node Modules/solution.js

pitfalls: SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module means "type": "module" is missing from package.json.
The package name in the import string must match the npm name exactly, including case (the reference solution has an import of "sillyName" with a capital N that would fail on case-sensitive systems).
The latest superheroes version uses a named export, so superheroes.random() fails; use randomSuperhero().
Run npm commands from the project folder or package.json lands in the wrong place.

gaps_and_ideas: Proposed lesson 'npm and packages' (blurb: install a package, read package.json, switch to ES modules). Tasks: 1) run npm init -y, 2) npm i a small package, 3) set type module and import it, 4) delete node_modules and restore with npm i, 5) swap require for import.
Starter idea: empty package.json plus an index.js with a commented-out require line.
Interactive demo idea: a simulated terminal that shows package.json and node_modules growing as commands are typed, with a toggle showing the CJS vs ESM syntax for the same call.

Teach the named-import form for superheroes (import { randomSuperhero } from "superheroes") and include a check task where the learner fixes a broken default import, since the reference repo's solution.js still uses the outdated default import.
